I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of watching strangers' lives through windows during evening walks.

---

There's a particular hour in early autumn when the sky turns that specific shade of blue that photographers call "magic hour" but which feels more like melancholy made visible. Streetlights flicker on, not yet necessary but preparing themselves. And in the houses I pass, people haven't drawn their curtains yet, or perhaps they've deliberately left them open, wanting that last bit of natural light, or wanting, unconsciously, to be seen.

I've been walking the same neighborhood for three years now, and I've developed what I can only call relationships with people I don't know. Not the kind where we'd recognize each other on the street—I'm careful to look away when actual encounters happen—but something more one-sided and therefore more honest, perhaps. The woman in the Craftsman on Birch Street who practices piano every Tuesday at 6:30. I don't know her name, but I know she struggles with the same Chopin nocturne, getting slightly further each week, and I feel a ridiculous pride when she finally masters a passage I'd been silently rooting for. The elderly couple on Elm who eat dinner at a small table pushed against their front window, always with a candle between them, always talking, never looking at phones. I wonder sometimes if they know they're performing a kind of art, this sustained attention in an age of distraction.

There's a guilt to this, of course. I'm aware I'm trespassing. But windows are architectural invitations, aren't they? The word itself comes from "wind eye"—an opening to let light and air enter, but also, inevitably, to let sight escape. We build these transparent walls and then act surprised when people look through them. The theater of domestic life has always used windows as its proscenium arch.

I think about this more now that I work from home, spending hours in rooms that face the street. I am, I realize, also on display. The UPS driver has seen me in pajamas at 2 PM. The dog walkers have witnessed my frustrated gestures during video calls. A teenager once watched me cry while chopping onions—though perhaps he thought the tears were for something else, some hidden grief he could imagine for me. We are all, in our lit rooms, unwitting actors in other people's private cinemas.

What strikes me most is how ordinary the tableaus are, and how this ordinariness becomes, with attention, extraordinary. The man assembling IKEA furniture with patient frustration. The child doing homework at a kitchen table, chin in hand, swinging one leg. Someone folding laundry with the television's blue flicker washing over them. These are the moments that never make it to social media, that resist narrative, that exist in the spaces between events we deem significant. Yet they're what life actually consists of, this accumulation of small maintained rituals, of tasks performed without applause.

I read once that the invention of electric light transformed the city into something unprecedented: a place where private life became visible after dark. Before, the night had been uniformly black, public and private equally obscured. Now we have these illuminated cells, these human aquariums, and we've never quite decided what the etiquette should be. Some cities have traditions—the Dutch apparently consider curtainless windows a matter of proud transparency, while in other cultures, the exposed lit room is unthinkable. We're still negotiating the terms of this visibility, still figuring out how to be seen and unseen simultaneously.

The pandemic changed something in this dynamic. For months, the window was the only theater available, the only way to feel connected to the ongoingness of others. I remember walking during lockdown with a desperate hunger for these glimpses, any proof that other lives continued in parallel to my own isolation. The woman on Birch Street played piano more often then, I noticed. The elderly couple on Elm started eating lunch at that window table too, perhaps needing the comfort of their ritual doubled. We were all more visible to each other, more needy of that confirmation, and somehow less embarrassed about it.

There's a phrase in Japanese, "komorebi," for the way sunlight filters through tree leaves. We need more words for the specific lights that filter through human lives: the laptop glow on a face at midnight, the warm kitchen light that makes a figure into a silhouette of purposeful movement, the sudden blue of a television changing a room's mood. These are the lights by which we increasingly know each other, mediated, partial, but not therefore false.

I wonder sometimes what my walkers see, what story they construct for the figure in the upstairs window, typing late, occasionally standing to stretch or stare out at nothing they can name. I hope they see someone trying, someone in the middle of a life that doesn't have a clear shape yet, someone who looks back at them looking in, this mutual regard that requires no names, no resolution, just the fact of being witness and witnessed, the oldest human contract there is.

The curtains are going up now, earlier as the evenings darken. Soon I'll lose my Tuesday concerts, my candlelit dinners, my silent domestic epics. But I'll keep walking, keep looking, keep being looked at in turn. The windows will stay, waiting for spring, waiting for that hour when the blue returns and we remember how to be visible to each other again, how to let the light out, how to make of our ordinary evenings something that might, with the right attention, be worth watching.
